extracted.intended_audience: magazine journalists, editors, fact-checkers, and news organizations covering campus sexual assault
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and best practices for investigative and magazine reporting about campus sexual assault, including editorial, fact-checking, legal, and victim-sensitivity considerations. Emphasizes verification, institutional accountability, and transparent attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely-warnings obligation under federal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities have an obligation under federal law to issue timely warnings when there is a 'serious or continuing' threat to student safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is credible information about multiple acts of sexual violence by the same perpetrator that may put students at risk, Department of Education guidelines indicate the university should take action even when no formal complaint has been filed and should consider issuing a public safety warning. Whether an institution should have issued a warning is reviewable against these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim confidentiality and autonomy (Dept. of Education guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines stress victim confidentiality and autonomy, meaning survivors decide whether to report and what assistance they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits what universities can do if a survivor does not identify individuals or organizations; reporters must understand these constraints when assessing institutional responses and public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA limits on disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) protects student privacy and can make it difficult for university staff to release records or answer questions about any enrollee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should know FERPA exceptions and work-arounds (e.g., students at public universities can sign privacy waivers; FERPA exception allows release of name/violation/sanction after final disposition). FERPA often restricts what administrators can say; plan reporting accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must push for thorough reporting (no shortcuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should insist on more phone calls, more travel, more time, until the reporting is complete rather than accepting gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative reporters and editors can have blind spots; it is the editor's duty to press the reporter to close gaps (contact witnesses, corroborate key claims) rather than accept unverified narrative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid investing a publication's reputation in a single source
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not base a major story primarily on one source without robust independent verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine 'invested Rolling Stone’s reputation in a single source' — this anti-pattern led to failure. Editors and fact-checkers should require corroboration before elevating single-source accounts into definitive narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudonyms should be rare and carefully reviewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Pseudonyms are 'inherently undesirable in journalism' and their use should be case-by-case, rare, and only after robust discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pseudonyms can introduce fictional-seeming elements and allow evasion of reporting gaps. If used, require convening, documentation of alternatives considered, and explicit discussion of risks and attribution to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checkers must be empowered to challenge writers and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checkers should be able to question and challenge decisions of writers and senior editors, and to escalate concerns to their supervisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checkers typically verify dates, descriptions, and attribution and should speak with sources (including confidential ones) to confirm facts. They must be given institutional 'muscle' and instruction to come forward when they find problems; failure to escalate undermines accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine confrontation of subjects with specific derogatory details
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and checkers should routinely share specific, derogatory details of an intended publication with the subjects to give them an opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the case described, editors did not give Phi Kappa Psi enough detail to challenge the account. Policies should expect that specific allegations be presented to subjects for comment unless there is a compelling reason not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking derogatory information with named sources/witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Derogatory or potentially reputation-damaging information must be checked with the individuals implicated or with independent witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the three friends whose lines appeared in the story were never contacted; 'Drew' (a lifeguard) was not verified. Fact-checkers and editors should ensure such people are reached or clearly disclose lack of verification to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance sensitivity to victims with rigorous verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should balance trauma-informed interviewing and survivors' desire for control with the journalistic need for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the terms of the reporter-survivor compact explicit (what documentation and corroboration will be sought, whether accused will be contacted). Allow survivors control over time/place/pace, but explain verification needs; be prepared to walk away if the survivor will not permit necessary verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate survivor accounts using available evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Track down corroborating evidence such as hospital records, 911 calls, texts, emails, security or phone video, and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many campus assaults have witnesses and early signals; reporters should seek hospital records, messages sent immediately after the assault, and bystanders. If inconsistencies exist, explain them in the reporting and consider trauma's effect on memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus reporting on institutional response when guilt cannot be proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic value often lies in analyzing how institutions respond to accusations rather than proving guilt or innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting on institutional policies, practices, and failures (Title IX compliance, adjudication systems, warnings) can be both impactful and less legally risky than trying to determine criminal culpability without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the legal and regulatory framework (Title IX, Clery, VAWA, OCR directives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must gain a deep understanding of the tangle of rules and guidelines governing campus sexual assault (Title IX, Clery Act, Violence Against Women Act, Office for Civil Rights directives, White House recommendations, state laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This knowledge helps reporters evaluate institutional conduct and know what information institutions are required or permitted to disclose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency with readers about what is known and unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit to readers about uncertainties, unverified details, and the origin of quotations or narrative passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a source's account supplies dialogue or there are unverified characters, disclose that to readers. Failure to make clear what is verified (e.g., that 'Drew' was unverified) misleads and exacerbates reporting failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking scope and duties in magazine journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazine fact-checkers review drafts to double-check dates, descriptions, attribution, and whether negatively depicted subjects have had their say; they may need to contact confidential sources and verify quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checkers should not be passive; they should push for verification, mark problems in drafts, and bring issues to their managers. They must be empowered institutionally to override or escalate when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal pre-publication review is standard but limited by privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: In-house counsel typically conducts pre-publication legal review, which is a standard part of the publication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal review may be protective but details of what counsel raised can be withheld under attorney-client privilege; editors should still ensure legal review addresses factual verifiability of allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against confirmation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors must be alert to the tendency to select facts that confirm pre-existing assumptions and to overlook contradictory information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek disconfirming evidence, track alternative narratives, and consider how institutional skepticism or sympathy may color reporting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make editorial policies clear on pseudonyms, attribution, and checking practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications should have clearer, stronger policies about when to use pseudonyms, how to check derogatory information, and whether to present specific details to subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than treating these decisions as ad-hoc, require explicit discussion, documentation, and dissent when necessary; adopt written guidelines to avoid inconsistent practice.
